Run the preflight check:

slides.subtitle: An occupancy grid turns a floor plan into cells a planner can search.
notes: • Part 2: Maps as graphs.
• Time: 20 min for this block, until 10:45 a.m..
• Part 1 builds the map every later step searches.

slides.title: Maps are grids of free and wall cells
body: Split the floor into equal square cells
Each cell is free or blocked: one bit each
Our map: 12 rows by 20 columns, # is a wall
Smaller cells: more detail, slower search
notes: • Show the warehouse map file; ask what each character means.
• A real robot builds this grid from its lidar; today we read it from a text file.
• Cell size is the first engineering choice: too big and narrow doors disappear.

slides.title: Neighbors make the grid a graph
body: Every free cell is a node
A step to a free neighbor is an edge
Four neighbors: up, down, left, right
Diagonals: only if no wall corner is cut
notes: • Draw one cell and its four neighbors on the board.
• Once it is a graph, every graph search algorithm applies.
• Ask: why must a diagonal step check both side cells?

slides.title: Demo: A grid in code
body: Run: python3 grid.py
What to watch for:
Row and column order: (row, col)
Start and goal found in the file
The start has only two free neighbors
notes: • Run grid.py from the solution folder and read the output aloud.
• Point out that row 0 is the top of the file.
• Fallback: the expected output is in the module README if the projector fails.

slides.title: neighbors() in 12 lines
notes: • This is the shape of the answer, without the corner rule.
• is_free() checks the bounds first, so we never index outside the map.
• The corner-cutting rule for diagonals is the stretch goal.

slides.subtitle: A* finds the shortest path by expanding the most promising cell first.
notes: • Part 3: A* search.
• Time: 15 min for this block, until 11:45 a.m..
• Part 2 turns the map into a shortest path.

slides.title: Blind search explores everything
body: Expand cells in order of distance from the start
Finds the shortest path, eventually
Our map: 100 cells expanded for a 32-step path
No idea where the goal is
notes: • Animate a ripple spreading from the start on the board.
• Dijkstra's algorithm is the same idea with step costs; on this grid they agree.
• The 100 cells come from astar.py with the zero heuristic.

slides.title: Heuristics aim the search at the goal
body: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
g: cost so far
h: estimate of the cost to go
Always expand the lowest f first
Manhattan distance: 60 cells, same 32 steps
notes: • Write f = g + h on the board and leave it there.
• Same path length, 40% fewer cells: that is the payoff.
• Ask: what happens if h is always zero?

slides.title: Admissible heuristics keep A* optimal
body: Admissible: never overestimates the true cost
Manhattan is exact for 4-way moves
With diagonals, use straight-line distance
Overestimate: faster, but paths can be longer
notes: • Admissible means optimistic: the estimate is never worse than reality.
• Manhattan overestimates once diagonal moves are allowed; that is the stretch goal.
• Engineers sometimes trade optimality for speed on purpose (weighted A*).

slides.title: The A* loop
notes: • Walk through one iteration with the board drawing.
• The heap always hands back the lowest f; ties break on g.
• The ... is exactly what they write in the activity.

slides.subtitle: A robot follows waypoints: simplify the path, then steer toward a point ahead.
notes: • Part 4: From path to motion.
• Time: 10 min for this block, until 1:05 p.m..
• Part 3 turns the path into motion a robot can follow.

slides.title: Grid paths zigzag: keep the corners
body: A* returns every cell: 33 of them
A robot needs only the turns: 12 waypoints
Keep a cell where the direction changes
Fewer waypoints, smoother driving
notes: • Show the 33-cell path, then the 12 corners, side by side.
• simplify() is step 1 of the activity.
• Real planners also smooth curves; corners are enough for today.

slides.title: Pure pursuit aims at a point ahead
body: Aim at a waypoint a short distance ahead
Turn toward it, at a limited rate
Move forward a little; repeat each tick
Look-ahead too short: wobble; too long: cut corners
notes: • Act it out: walk toward a point ahead of you and keep re-aiming.
• The turn limit is what makes it a robot rather than a teleport.
• The stretch goal is tuning the look-ahead distance.

slides.title: One tick of the controller

textboxes.text:
target, index = lookahead_point(
    waypoints, index, (x, y), lookahead)
heading = steer(heading, (x, y), target, max_turn)
x += speed * math.cos(heading)
y += speed * math.sin(heading)
if grid[int(y)][int(x)]:
    crashed = True

notes: • Three lines do the work: pick a target, turn, move.
• x is the column and y the row, so the map is not flipped.
• The crash check is the test they need to pass.
